segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a man from among the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a leader of the Jews.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came to Jesus by night and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born from above, they cannot see the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nicodemus said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How can a person be born when already old? Surely no one can enter their mother’s womb a second time and be born?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless someone is born of water and Spirit, they cannot enter the kingdom of God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do not be amazed that I told you, ‘You must be born from above.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Nicodemus answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “How can these things happen?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You are the teacher of Israel, and you do not understand these things?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly, truly, I tell you, we speak of what we know and testify to what we have seen, yet you do not accept our testimony.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If I have told you about earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you about heavenly things?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And no one has gone up into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that everyone who believes may have eternal life in him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has been judged already, because they have not believed in the name of the one and only Son of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light, because their deeds were evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For everyone who does what is base hates the light and does not come to the light, so that their deeds may not be exposed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that their deeds may be shown to have been done in God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and there he spent time with them and was baptizing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was plenty of water there, and people were coming and being baptized;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for John had not yet been thrown into prison.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then a dispute arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew about purification.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They came to John and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Rabbi, the one who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you have testified—look, he is baptizing, and everyone is going to him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “No one can receive even one thing unless it has been given to them from heaven.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: You yourselves testify for me that I said, ‘I am not the Messiah,’ but, ‘I have been sent ahead of him.’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. But the bridegroom’s friend, who stands and listens to him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. So this joy of mine is now complete.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: He must increase, and I must decrease.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who comes from above is above all. The one who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth. The one who comes from heaven is above all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He testifies to what he has seen and heard, yet no one accepts his testimony.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever has accepted his testimony has set their seal to this, that God is true.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one whom God sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever disobeys the Son will not see life; rather, the wrath of God remains on them.

notes.note: The Greek word can mean either “from above” or “again,” and the dialogue plays on both: Nicodemus hears “a second time” (verse 4), while Jesus goes on to speak of birth from the Spirit. Elsewhere in John, including verse 31 of this chapter, the word always means “from above,” so that sense is given here. Many translations keep “born again,” and scholars widely agree that the double meaning is deliberate.

notes.phrase: You must be born from above
notes.note: The “you” inside this quotation is plural in Greek, as it is in “you do not accept” (verse 11) and throughout verse 12. Jesus is addressing Nicodemus as the representative of a group, just as Nicodemus began with “we know” in verse 2.

The same Greek word means “wind,” “breath,” and “spirit,” and it is the word translated “Spirit” in verses 5, 6, and at the end of this verse. Likewise the word for the wind’s “sound” also means “voice.” The comparison is therefore a wordplay that English cannot reproduce: the Spirit, like the wind, is known by its effects and not by its origin or destination.

notes.traditional: the Son of man which is in heaven
notes.note: Many later manuscripts add “who is in heaven” after “the Son of Man,” and the King James Version includes it. The earliest surviving manuscripts lack the phrase, and the Greek text translated here omits it, though some scholars defend it as original.

The allusion is to Numbers 21:4–9, where Moses set a bronze snake on a pole and those bitten by snakes looked at it and lived. The verb also means “exalt,” and John uses it with both senses at once (see 8:28; 12:32–34): Jesus’ being raised on the cross is at the same time his exaltation.

The adjective is formed from the word for “age.” In Jewish usage of the period “eternal life” meant the life of the age to come, so it describes a kind of life as well as an unending one. In John this life is something the believer already has (verse 36).

The phrase “in him” can be attached either to “believes” or to “have eternal life.” John normally writes “believe in” with a different preposition (as in verse 16), so here the phrase is taken with “have eternal life.” Many translations read “everyone who believes in him may have eternal life,” and some manuscripts have the wording that favors that reading.

notes.phrase: For God so loved the world
notes.note: Ancient manuscripts had no quotation marks, and it is disputed where Jesus’ words to Nicodemus end. This translation closes the speech at verse 15 and treats verses 16–21 as the evangelist’s reflection, because the language shifts to the past tense and to terms characteristic of the narrator, such as “one and only Son.” Many translations and scholars instead continue Jesus’ speech through verse 21.

The Greek word means “only one of its kind” and was the ordinary term for an only child; its second element comes from the word for “kind,” not the verb “beget.” “One and only” or “only” is the rendering of most modern translations, though a minority of scholars have recently defended “only begotten.”

Most English versions render the verb “condemn” in verses 17–18 and then switch to “judgment” or “verdict” for the related noun in verse 19. The Greek uses one word family throughout, and “judge” and “judgment” keep that link visible. The context makes clear that an unfavorable judgment is meant, which is why “condemn” is the common choice.

The Greek word, traditionally “Christ,” translates the Hebrew title “Messiah,” the anointed king Israel expected. Here John is denying a title, not a name, so “Messiah” is used. Several modern translations make the same distinction, using “Messiah” where the title is under discussion in the Gospels and “Christ” elsewhere.

notes.phrase: The one who comes from above
notes.note: As with verse 16, it is uncertain who is speaking in verses 31–36. This translation ends John the Baptist’s words at verse 30 and takes the rest as the evangelist’s comment, since the passage echoes the language of verses 11–18. Some translations and scholars treat it as the continuation of John’s speech.

notes.phrase: he gives the Spirit without measure
notes.traditional: God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him
notes.note: The Greek does not state who gives or who receives. Most interpreters understand that God gives the Spirit without limit to the one he sent, and some manuscripts and translations make this explicit by adding “God” or “to him.” It is also possible to read the one sent as the giver of the Spirit.

candidates.reason: Translations vary between “judge” and “condemn” (and “judgment,” “verdict,” “condemnation” for κρίσις), which hides the word family across John, Paul and the Synoptics.
Capitalization and the choice between Spirit, spirit, wind and breath recur throughout the New Testament and need a single policy.
Translators split between “flesh,” “human nature,” and “sinful nature,” especially in Paul, and readers are misled if the English varies.
A key term in John and Acts that is rendered variously as “testify,” “bear witness,” and “witness”; the verb and the noun μαρτυρία should match.
Translations vary between “disobey,” “reject,” and “not believe” across John, Acts, Romans, Hebrews and 1 Peter, which obscures the relation between unbelief and disobedience.
